- ✗ **A. One VM per part:** VMs give full control, but each one has its own operating system to patch and manage and is heavier and slower to start than a container, which is what the team wants to avoid.
- ✓ **B. Containers (correct):** each part of the website is packaged with its dependencies, starts quickly, can run alongside others on one host and has no per-container operating system to manage, and each part scales or updates independently without a rewrite.
- ✗ **C. Azure Functions:** Functions run event-triggered code that finishes quickly; moving the website onto them means rewriting it, which the requirement rules out.
- ✗ **D. Scale set running everything together:** every instance carries all three parts and its own operating system, so the parts cannot be scaled or updated separately and the team still manages VMs.

## Key idea
Packaging independent parts of an app with their dependencies, many per host and with no operating system to manage for each, points to containers.
Q006510:
## Grouping VMs
Running one VM is fine for testing. Production workloads usually group VMs, and Azure offers two features with different goals:
- **Virtual Machine Scale Sets** create and manage a group of **identical, load-balanced VMs**. Autoscale rules add instances when demand rises (for example CPU above a threshold, or on a schedule) and remove them when it falls. Configuration stays consistent because every instance comes from the same model.
- **Availability sets** spread a fixed set of VMs across **fault domains** (separate power and network) and **update domains** (rebooted at different times during maintenance). They improve resiliency but never add or remove VMs.
## The VM is still IaaS
With either feature the workload stays on VMs, so the company keeps full control of the operating system, which is why it suits an app that needs specific OS settings.
Example: a scale set that holds 2 instances normally and grows to 20 when CPU stays above 70 percent in the week before the deadline.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Virtual Machine Scale Sets (correct):** they run identical VMs from one configuration, add and remove instances automatically with demand or a schedule, and work with a load balancer to spread traffic, while the app keeps its custom OS settings.
- ✗ **B. Availability set:** it spreads a fixed number of VMs across fault and update domains for resiliency, but it has no autoscale, so the extra capacity for the peaks would still have to be added by hand.
- ✗ **C. Azure Virtual Desktop:** it delivers Windows desktops and apps to users, not a scalable back end that serves the filing service's customers through a web application.
- ✗ **D. Container instances per customer:** the application is built for Windows VMs with specific OS settings, and starting a container per customer is not a load-balanced web tier for the service.

## Key idea
Identical VMs that grow and shrink automatically with demand point to Virtual Machine Scale Sets; availability sets only add resiliency.
Q006511:
## Desktop and app virtualization
**Azure Virtual Desktop** runs Windows desktops and applications in Azure and streams them to users on almost any device. Key points:
- Desktops and apps are managed centrally by IT, so every user gets the same standardized environment.
- Apps and data stay in Azure-hosted sessions, which reduces data exposure on local and personal devices.
- It supports single-session and **multi-session** Windows, so several users can share one VM.
- It integrates with Microsoft Entra ID for identity and access controls, such as Conditional Access and multifactor authentication.
## Why not just build VMs
You could create one VM per user, but you would manage each one separately and expose many RDP endpoints. Azure Virtual Desktop is the managed way to give many users a full desktop.
Example: 200 seasonal agents sign in from their laptops and get the call-center desktop; when the season ends, IT removes their access and no company data is left on the laptops.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. App Service web apps:** App Service hosts web applications and APIs; it does not give users a full Windows desktop or run the company's desktop applications.
- ✗ **B. One public VM per agent:** this is a full desktop, but every VM must be managed separately and each one exposes RDP to the internet, which is the opposite of centralized and secure.
- ✓ **C. Azure Virtual Desktop (correct):** it delivers full Windows desktops and apps from Azure to personal devices, keeps the data in Azure sessions and lets IT manage the desktops centrally.
- ✗ **D. Entra Domain Services:** it offers managed domain join, LDAP and Kerberos for Azure workloads, but it provides no desktops, and joining personal laptops to a domain does not keep data off them.

## Key idea
Centrally managed Windows desktops and apps delivered from Azure to any device are Azure Virtual Desktop.
Q006512:
## Connecting networks in Azure
- **Virtual network peering** links two virtual networks directly. Traffic between peered networks stays private on the Microsoft backbone and never enters the public internet. Peered networks can be in different regions (global peering).
- **Azure VPN Gateway** sends encrypted traffic between an Azure virtual network and another location **over the public internet**:
- *site-to-site*: an on-premises VPN device to the Azure gateway (whole office);
- *point-to-site*: one computer to the Azure gateway.
- **Azure ExpressRoute** is a dedicated private connection through a connectivity provider that does **not** go over the internet, for predictable performance and higher bandwidth.
## Related services that do not connect networks
- **Azure DNS** (including private DNS zones) resolves names; it carries no traffic.
- A **private endpoint** gives one Azure service, such as a storage account, a private IP inside a virtual network; it does not join two networks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. ExpressRoute:** it is a private connection through a connectivity provider that deliberately avoids the internet, so it does not use the office's existing internet link and needs a new provider circuit.
- ✗ **B. Private DNS zone:** it lets resources resolve custom names inside the networks, but name resolution moves no traffic and creates no connection between the networks or the office.
- ✗ **C. Private endpoints:** a private endpoint brings a single Azure service into a virtual network with a private IP; it cannot be used to connect one virtual network to another.
- ✓ **D. Global virtual network peering (correct):** it connects the two virtual networks directly, even across regions, and their traffic stays private on the Microsoft backbone.
- ✓ **E. VPN Gateway site-to-site (correct):** it builds an encrypted tunnel from the office's VPN device to the East US network over the internet link the office already has.

## Key idea
Network to network inside Azure: peering. Office over the internet, encrypted: VPN Gateway. Private line that avoids the internet: ExpressRoute.
Q006513:
## Public and private endpoints
- A **public endpoint** has a public IP address and can be reached from anywhere in the world (subject to the service's firewall rules). Azure PaaS services such as Azure Storage and Azure SQL Database have one by default.
- A **private endpoint** is a network interface with a **private IP address from your virtual network's subnet**. It connects privately to one service (through Azure Private Link), in effect bringing that service into your virtual network.
## Using a private endpoint
After creating it, clients in the virtual network (and connected networks over VPN or ExpressRoute) resolve the service's name to the private IP, for example `mystorage.blob.core.windows.net` to `10.1.2.5`. You can then disable public network access on the storage account so only private traffic is accepted.
Example: a private endpoint for the account's blob service in subnet `snet-data` gets address `10.1.2.5`; the VMs keep using the normal blob URL, and the account rejects requests from the internet.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Private endpoint (correct):** it places a network interface with a private IP from the virtual network in front of the storage account, so the VMs reach it privately and the public endpoint can be switched off.
- ✗ **B. Peering with the storage account:** peering connects two virtual networks. A storage account is not deployed in a virtual network, so there is nothing to peer with.
- ✗ **C. NSG rule to the public endpoint:** the traffic would still go to the account's public endpoint, so public network access could not be disabled and no private IP from the virtual network is involved.
- ✗ **D. Private DNS zone alone:** a DNS zone only maps names to addresses; without a private endpoint, the name would still point to the public endpoint, which must stay open.

## Key idea
To reach a PaaS service through a private IP in your virtual network and close its public access, create a private endpoint.
Q006514:
## Blob access tiers
Azure Blob Storage lets you choose a tier per blob to balance storage cost against access cost:
- **Hot** (online): data in active use. Highest storage cost, lowest access cost.
- **Cool** (online): infrequently accessed data, stored for at least 30 days.
- **Cold** (online): rarely accessed data that still needs fast retrieval, stored for at least 90 days.
- **Archive** (offline): rarely accessed data that tolerates hours of latency, stored for at least 180 days. Lowest storage cost, highest retrieval cost.
Moving or deleting a blob before its tier's minimum period causes an early deletion charge.
## Archive is offline
A blob in the archive tier cannot be read directly. You first **rehydrate** it to hot, cool or cold, which takes hours (up to 15 hours with standard priority for most blobs). That is acceptable when hours of delay are fine.
Example: a lifecycle management rule moves case files to archive after 30 days; when a lawyer needs a file, it is rehydrated to the cool tier and read a few hours later.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cool tier:** it is an online tier for data read occasionally, and its storage cost is higher than both cold and archive, so it is not the cheapest place for files that sit untouched for years.
- ✓ **B. Archive tier (correct):** it has the lowest storage cost of all tiers and suits data kept for years that is rarely read, and the firm can accept the hours-long rehydration before a file is available.
- ✗ **C. Hot tier:** it is optimized for data in active use and has the highest storage cost, which is the wrong trade-off for files that are almost never read.
- ✗ **D. Cold tier:** it is online and returns data immediately, but its storage cost is higher than archive; paying for instant access the firm does not need is not the lowest cost.

## Key idea
Rarely read data that can wait hours for retrieval belongs in the archive tier, the cheapest place to store it.
Q006515:
## How Azure Storage keeps copies
Azure Storage always keeps several copies of your data. The redundancy option decides where:
- **LRS**: three copies in one datacenter of the primary region. Protects against drive, server and rack failures, not against losing the datacenter.
- **ZRS**: copies spread synchronously across availability zones of the primary region. Reads and writes continue if one zone fails.
- **GRS**: LRS in the primary region plus asynchronous replication to the secondary region (kept there as LRS).
- **GZRS**: ZRS in the primary region plus asynchronous replication to the secondary region.
- **RA-GRS / RA-GZRS**: the same as GRS / GZRS, plus read access to the secondary copy at any time.
## Two different failures
A zone failure is handled inside the primary region (needs ZRS or GZRS). A regional disaster needs a secondary copy (needs GRS or GZRS). Only GZRS (or RA-GZRS) covers both.
Example: an `orders` account with GZRS in a zone-enabled region keeps working when zone 2 fails and still has a copy in the secondary region if the primary region is lost.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. ZRS:** it survives a zone failure, but every copy stays in the primary region, so a disaster that takes out the region leaves no second-region copy.
- ✗ **B. LRS:** all three copies sit in one datacenter, so a zone failure can make the data unavailable, and there is no copy in another region.
- ✗ **C. GRS:** it has a secondary-region copy, but the primary region uses LRS, which is not spread across zones for availability, so a zone outage can stop access until the company fails over.
- ✓ **D. GZRS (correct):** ZRS in the primary region keeps the data readable and writable through a zone failure, and asynchronous replication to the secondary region protects against losing the whole primary region.

## Key idea
Zone outages need ZRS in the primary region; regional disasters need geo-replication; GZRS combines both.
Q006516:
## Tools for moving and syncing files
- **AzCopy**: a command-line tool that copies blobs or files to, from and between storage accounts. Its sync is **one-directional**: you name a source and a destination.
- **Azure Storage Explorer**: a graphical app for Windows, macOS and Linux that manages blobs and files; it uses AzCopy underneath.
- **Azure File Sync**: centralizes file shares in Azure Files while keeping Windows file servers as local caches. An agent on Windows Server keeps the server **bi-directionally** in sync with the Azure file share.
## What Azure File Sync adds
- Users keep accessing files locally through protocols on Windows Server such as SMB.
- **Cloud tiering** keeps frequently used files on the local server and leaves rarely used files in Azure until someone opens them.
- You can have caches in many offices, and replace a failed server by installing Azure File Sync on a new one.
Example: the Seoul and Busan offices both cache the `projects` share from the same Azure file share; a change in Seoul appears in Busan after it syncs through Azure.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Scheduled AzCopy:** AzCopy synchronizes in one direction only and has no local caching or cloud tiering, so changes made in Azure or in other branches would not flow back to each office.
- ✗ **B. Azure Data Box:** it moves large data sets with a shipped physical device, typically once; it does not keep file servers synchronized with Azure on an ongoing basis.
- ✓ **C. Azure File Sync (correct):** it keeps each branch's Windows Server synchronized with Azure Files in both directions and uses cloud tiering to cache hot files locally while cold files stay in Azure.
- ✗ **D. Azure Migrate:** it assesses and migrates servers, databases and web apps to Azure. Moving the file servers to Azure VMs would remove the local caches the branches need.

## Key idea
Centralize shares in Azure Files while keeping Windows file servers as local caches: Azure File Sync.
Q006517:
## Online and offline data transfer
Most transfers go over the network with tools such as AzCopy or Azure Storage Explorer. When the data set is very large and bandwidth is limited, the network becomes the bottleneck.
**Azure Data Box** is a physical (offline) transfer service:
- You order the device in the Azure portal; a carrier delivers it to your site.
- You copy the data to it over your local network, then ship it back.
- Microsoft uploads the data into your storage account, and the device's disks are then securely wiped.
- It also works in the other direction, for exporting data out of Azure.
Typical uses: one-time bulk migrations, periodic large uploads where online transfer is too slow, and exporting large data sets.
## Not the same as Azure Migrate
**Azure Migrate** is a hub for discovering, assessing and migrating servers, databases and web apps. It helps move workloads, not a one-off pile of files over a slow link.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Azure Data Box (correct):** copying tens of terabytes onto a shipped device avoids the slow internet link entirely and suits a one-time bulk transfer with no ongoing sync.
- ✗ **B. Azure Storage Explorer:** it uploads over the internet connection, so moving tens of terabytes would still take the many weeks the lab wants to avoid.
- ✗ **C. Azure Migrate:** it assesses and migrates servers, databases and web apps to Azure; it is not a way to ship a large set of image files past a slow network.
- ✗ **D. Azure File Sync:** it keeps Windows file servers and Azure Files in sync over the network, so the slow link remains the bottleneck and the lab does not need ongoing sync.

## Key idea
Very large, one-time transfers over limited bandwidth point to Azure Data Box, an offline device shipped by Microsoft.
Q006518:
## Everyday file movement tools
- **AzCopy** is a command-line utility for copying blobs or files to or from a storage account, and between storage accounts. Example: `azcopy copy "C:\reports" "https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/reports" --recursive`. Its sync is one-directional.
- **Azure Storage Explorer** is a standalone app for Windows, macOS and Linux with a graphical interface. You can upload, download and move data between storage accounts. It uses AzCopy underneath.
## Tools with a different purpose
- **Azure File Sync** keeps on-premises Windows file servers synchronized with Azure Files shares, with optional cloud tiering.
- **Azure Migrate** is a hub for discovering, assessing and migrating servers, databases and web apps.
- **Azure Data Box** moves very large data sets offline on a shipped device.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Azure Data Box:** it is meant for very large offline transfers on a shipped device; it is far too heavy for a folder upload and does not copy between storage accounts.
- ✓ **B. Azure Storage Explorer (correct):** it does the same uploads and account-to-account copies through a graphical interface, using AzCopy behind the scenes.
- ✗ **C. Azure Migrate:** it moves whole workloads such as servers, databases and web apps, not individual folders and blobs from an administrator's workstation.
- ✗ **D. Azure File Sync:** it synchronizes Windows Server with Azure file shares, not a one-off upload to a blob container or a copy between two accounts.
- ✓ **E. AzCopy (correct):** it copies files to blob containers and blobs between storage accounts from the command line, which covers both tasks and can be scripted.

## Key idea
For everyday uploads and account-to-account copies use AzCopy (command line) or Azure Storage Explorer (graphical).
Q006519:
## Signals, decisions, enforcement
**Conditional Access** is a Microsoft Entra ID feature that decides how a sign-in is handled based on signals:
- **Signals**: who the user is, their location or IP range, the device, the app they are opening, the sign-in risk.
- **Decision**: allow, block, or allow only after an extra step.
- **Enforcement**: for example require multifactor authentication (MFA) or a compliant device.
Typical policies: require MFA for administrators, require MFA from outside trusted network locations, block sign-ins from unexpected countries, allow access to sensitive apps only from managed devices.
## Related features
- **Security defaults** turn on baseline protections (such as MFA registration) for the whole tenant in one switch, but they cannot be customized with your own location rules.
- **Azure RBAC** decides what an identity may do with Azure resources after it has signed in.
Example: a policy for all users and all cloud apps, excluding the named location `Head office`, requires MFA; a second policy blocks the countries the company does not operate in.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Just-in-time VM access:** this Defender for Cloud feature opens management ports on VMs for a limited time; it does not control how users sign in to Microsoft Entra ID.
- ✗ **B. Security defaults:** they apply a fixed set of baseline protections for the whole tenant and offer no custom rules such as trusted locations or blocked countries.
- ✓ **C. Conditional Access (correct):** it uses the sign-in location as a signal, so one policy can require MFA outside trusted network locations and another can block selected countries.
- ✗ **D. Azure RBAC:** role assignments grant permissions on Azure resources at a scope; they do not evaluate sign-in location or trigger multifactor authentication.

## Key idea
Location-, device- or risk-based sign-in rules such as "MFA outside the office" are Conditional Access policies.
Q006520:
## Azure role-based access control
**Azure RBAC** controls who can do what with Azure resources. A role assignment has three parts:
- **Security principal**: a user, group, service principal or managed identity.
- **Role definition**: a set of allowed actions, for example **Owner**, **Contributor**, **Reader**, or a specific built-in role such as **Virtual Machine Contributor** (create and manage VMs and their disks, but no management access to the virtual network or storage account they connect to, and no right to assign roles).
- **Scope**: a management group, subscription, resource group or single resource.
Permissions are **inherited downward**: a role at the subscription applies to every resource group and resource in it. Least privilege means choosing the narrowest role at the narrowest scope that still does the job.
## RBAC is not Entra roles or Azure Policy
- **Microsoft Entra roles** (for example Global Administrator) manage the directory: users, groups, tenant settings.
- **Azure Policy** checks and enforces rules about resource properties; it does not grant anyone permissions.
Example: role assignment = contractor + Virtual Machine Contributor + `/subscriptions/<id>/resourceGroups/rg-web`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Azure Policy grant:** Azure Policy evaluates and enforces rules on resource properties, such as allowed sizes or regions; it never grants permissions to a user.
- ✓ **B. Virtual Machine Contributor at rg-web (correct):** this role lets the contractor manage VMs, and the resource group scope keeps that permission out of every other resource group in the subscription.
- ✗ **C. Owner at the subscription:** it gives full control, including access management, over every resource in the subscription; asking the contractor to stay in rg-web is a promise, not a control.
- ✗ **D. Global Administrator:** it is the most powerful Microsoft Entra directory role, a huge over-grant, and it does not by itself grant access to Azure resources in the subscription.

## Key idea
Least privilege in Azure RBAC means the narrowest built-in role at the narrowest scope, here Virtual Machine Contributor on one resource group.
Q006521:
## Two kinds of directory
- **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure AD) is Microsoft's cloud identity service. It handles authentication with modern protocols, single sign-on, multifactor authentication, application management and device registration.
- **Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)** is the traditional Windows Server directory: domain join, Group Policy, LDAP, Kerberos and NTLM. Many legacy apps depend on it.
## Microsoft Entra Domain Services
It gives you a **managed domain** in Azure that offers AD DS features (domain join, Group Policy, LDAP, Kerberos/NTLM) without you running domain controllers. Azure deploys and maintains two Windows Server domain controllers (a replica set) and handles patching and backups.
- It synchronizes one way from Microsoft Entra ID, so users sign in with their existing credentials.
- In a hybrid setup, **Microsoft Entra Connect** syncs on-premises AD to Microsoft Entra ID, which then syncs to the managed domain.

## The Zero Trust model
Traditional security trusted anything inside the corporate network perimeter. **Zero Trust** assumes no network location is safe and evaluates every request. Its three guiding principles:
- **Verify explicitly**: always authenticate and authorize based on all available data points, such as identity, location, device health, service or workload, and anomalies.
- **Use least privilege access**: limit access with just-in-time and just-enough access (JIT/JEA), risk-based adaptive policies and data protection.
- **Assume breach**: minimize the blast radius by segmenting access, verify end-to-end encryption, and use analytics for visibility and threat detection.
## Zero Trust and defense in depth
**Defense in depth** is a different, complementary model: layers (physical security, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, data) each slow an attacker so that the data at the center stays protected.
Example: the same Conditional Access policy evaluates a sign-in from the office and from a coffee shop; the office network earns no extra trust.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Assume breach:** it focuses on limiting damage with segmentation, encryption and threat analytics, not on evaluating each sign-in's identity and device signals.
- ✗ **B. Use least privilege access:** it is about how much access is granted once a user is verified, such as just-in-time or just-enough permissions, not about checking every request.
- ✓ **C. Verify explicitly (correct):** checking identity, device health and risk on every access, regardless of where the laptop is connected, is authenticating and authorizing based on all available signals instead of the network location.
- ✗ **D. Defense in depth:** it is a separate layered security model, not one of the three Zero Trust principles, and the scenario describes checks on each request rather than layers.

## Key idea
"Never trust, always verify": checking identity, device and risk on every request wherever it comes from is the Zero Trust principle verify explicitly.

## Reliability as a cloud benefit
Microsoft defines **reliability** as the ability of a system to recover from failures and continue to function. It is also one of the pillars of the Azure Well-Architected Framework.
## Why the cloud helps
- The cloud has a **decentralized design**: you can deploy resources in regions around the world instead of in one building.

## What reliability does not mean
Reliability is not a promise that nothing fails. Hardware, software and whole sites can still fail; a reliable design expects failure and recovers from it. Microsoft notes that in some cases the cloud environment shifts to another region for you, but in general you design your applications to take advantage of the extra regions.
## Example
A booking service runs in two Azure regions. When a storm takes one region offline, users are served from the other region while the first one recovers.

- ✓ **A. Decentralized, global design (correct):** Microsoft ties cloud reliability to the ability to deploy resources in regions around the world, so that one region's catastrophic event does not stop the others.
- ✗ **B. No-outage guarantee:** no provider promises that nothing ever fails. Reliability is about recovering from failures, so customers still design for them.
- ✗ **C. Preconfigured templates:** templates support consistent deployments (governance and manageability), but they do not make a system resilient to a regional disaster.
- ✗ **D. Pay-as-you-go during outages:** consumption pricing is a cost benefit (operational expenditure), not a reason the infrastructure recovers from failures.

## Key idea
Cloud reliability comes from a decentralized, global design: resources in many regions let a system recover and keep working when one location fails.

## Scalability as a cloud benefit
**Scalability** is the ability to adjust resources to meet demand. Because the cloud is a consumption-based model, you only pay for what you use: when demand drops, you reduce resources and so reduce costs.
## Two directions of scaling
- **Vertical scaling** changes the **capabilities** of a resource. Scale **up** to add CPUs or RAM to a virtual machine; scale **down** by lowering the CPU or RAM specifications when you over-specified it.
- **Horizontal scaling** changes the **number** of resources. Scale **out** by adding virtual machines or containers when demand jumps; scale **in** by removing them when demand drops. It can be automatic or manual.
## Choosing
Horizontal scaling only helps if the work can be shared across instances. An app that must run on one machine needs a bigger machine: vertical scaling.
## Example
On the 28th the firm resizes its VM to a size with twice the memory; on the 3rd of the next month it resizes back to the original size and pays the higher rate only for those days.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Load balancer:** load balancing spreads requests across several resources; with a single VM there is nothing to spread to, and it does not add memory.
- ✓ **B. Vertical scaling (correct):** Microsoft describes scaling up as adding CPUs or RAM to a virtual machine and scaling down as lowering them again, which suits an app that must stay on one machine and needs more memory only at month-end.
- ✗ **C. Three-year reservation:** a reservation is a pricing commitment, not scaling; it keeps paying for the larger size all month, the opposite of reducing resources when demand drops.
- ✗ **D. Horizontal scale-out:** adding instances only helps when the work can be spread across machines, and this app cannot be split, so the extra VMs would sit idle.

## Key idea
Vertical scaling changes the size (CPU, RAM) of a resource; horizontal scaling changes the number of resources.

Handling DDoS attacks at a scale a small company cannot match is part of the security benefit of the cloud.

## Definitions, initiatives and assignments
Azure Policy has three main objects:
- **Policy definition**: one business rule written in JSON, with a condition and an **effect** (for example "storage accounts must not allow public access", effect Deny or Audit).
- **Initiative definition** (called a *policySet* in the Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell): a collection of policy definitions grouped toward one overarching goal, such as a security baseline.
- **Assignment**: a definition or initiative applied to a scope (management group, subscription, resource group or single resource).
## Why group into an initiative
An initiative is assigned and tracked as **one item**, and its compliance is reported as one overall state with per-policy detail. Microsoft recommends creating initiatives even when you start with one policy: when you later add a definition to the initiative, it automatically becomes part of the existing initiative assignments, so you do not multiply assignments.
## Example
Initiative `Security baseline` = "no public storage" + "require HTTPS" + "allowed VM SKUs" + ... → one assignment per subscription → one compliance view.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Policy exemption:** an exemption removes a resource or scope from evaluation of an assignment. It is the opposite of grouping rules to enforce them.
- ✓ **B. Policy initiative (correct):** an initiative groups related policy definitions toward one goal, is assigned as a single item, and definitions added later become part of the existing assignments automatically.
- ✗ **C. Management group:** a management group is a container for subscriptions. It is a scope you assign policies to, not something that holds or groups policy rules.
- ✗ **D. Custom RBAC role:** roles define which actions identities may perform. They cannot express rules about how resources must be configured or report compliance against them.

## Key idea
Group related policy definitions into an initiative to assign and track them as one compliance goal.
Q006545:
## Policy effects
Every policy definition has one **effect** that decides what happens when a resource matches the rule:
- **Audit**: creates a warning event in the activity log and marks the resource noncompliant, but does not stop the request.
- **Deny**: fails the create or update request (HTTP 403 Forbidden). Existing resources that match are marked noncompliant.
- **Modify**: adds, updates or removes properties or tags during create or update; existing resources can be fixed with a remediation task.
- **DeployIfNotExists**: deploys a related resource (through a template) when it is missing.
## Start with Audit
Microsoft's guidance is to begin with an audit effect instead of an enforcement effect (deny, modify, deployIfNotExists). You learn how many resources the rule would affect, and nothing breaks existing deployments or automation. When the results look right, you switch the effect to Deny.
## Example
Week 1: assign the rule with Audit → dashboard shows 14 noncompliant accounts → owners fix them → week 4: change the effect to Deny.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Audit (correct):** it reports which resources break the rule and logs a warning event, but never blocks a deployment, which is exactly a "measure first" rollout.
- ✗ **B. DeployIfNotExists:** it deploys extra resources when a related resource is missing. It is an enforcement action, not a report-only check.
- ✗ **C. Deny:** Deny rejects noncompliant create and update requests immediately, so teams would no longer deploy normally.
- ✗ **D. Modify:** Modify changes the resource during deployment. That alters what teams deploy instead of only reporting on it.

## Key idea
Roll out a new rule with the Audit effect to see its impact, then switch to Deny to enforce it.
Q006546:
## Fixing resources with Azure Policy
Some effects change resources instead of only reporting on them:
- **Modify** adds, replaces or removes tags (and certain properties) on a resource **while it is created or updated**. The built-in definition "Add a tag to resources" uses it.
- **DeployIfNotExists** deploys a missing related resource.
## Remediation of existing resources
Effects act when a request is made. Resources that already exist and break the rule are only marked noncompliant during evaluation. To bring them into line you create a **remediation task**, which applies the Modify operations (or the DeployIfNotExists template) to existing resources.
Remediation runs under a **managed identity** attached to the policy assignment, which needs an Azure role that allows the change.
## Example
Assign "Add a tag to resources" with `CostCenter=Unassigned` → new resources get the tag at creation → a remediation task tags the 300 older resources.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Deny:** Deny blocks new untagged requests but cannot add a default value, and it does not retag existing resources; they are only reported as noncompliant.
- ✗ **B. Delete lock:** a lock blocks deletion of resources. It has no notion of tags and cannot require or add them.
- ✗ **C. Audit:** Audit only marks resources noncompliant and logs a warning. It never adds or changes a tag, during evaluation or at any other time.
- ✓ **D. Modify with remediation (correct):** Modify adds the tag to new or updated resources automatically, and a remediation task applies the same change to resources that already exist.

## Key idea
To add a missing setting automatically, use the Modify (or DeployIfNotExists) effect, and run a remediation task to fix resources that already exist.
Q006547:
## Inheritance of assignments
A policy assignment applies to its scope and everything below it: an assignment on a subscription covers every resource group and resource in that subscription.
## Azure Policy is an explicit deny system
Assignments are evaluated **independently** and the result is cumulative, most restrictive. A more permissive assignment lower in the hierarchy does not cancel a Deny from above: if any assignment denies a resource, it is denied. The only way to allow it is to change the denying assignment.
## Excluding a scope
An assignment can list **excluded scopes** (`notScopes`): child resource groups or resources that the assignment does not evaluate. Microsoft's own example: assign "no networking resources" at the subscription, exclude the resource group intended for networking infrastructure, then give trusted users access to that group.
## Policy and RBAC are separate
RBAC controls who can act; Azure Policy controls what the resulting resource may look like. Even if a user may perform an action, Azure Policy still blocks a noncompliant create or update.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Newer assignment overrides:** assignments do not override each other by age or scope. Each one is evaluated, and any Deny still blocks the request.
- ✗ **B. ReadOnly lock:** a lock does not pause policy evaluation. It would block all changes in the group, including the deployments the team needs.
- ✓ **C. Exclude the resource group (correct):** the subscription-level Deny keeps applying until that group is listed as an excluded scope of the assignment; access for the network team is then controlled with RBAC.
- ✗ **D. Owner role:** Azure Policy evaluates the request regardless of the caller's role, so an Owner is denied just like anyone else.

## Key idea
Azure Policy denies are cumulative; to allow a child scope, exclude it from the denying assignment rather than adding a looser policy below it.
Q006548:
## How a request is checked
When someone creates or updates a resource, Azure Resource Manager checks the request in two separate ways:
- **Azure RBAC**: is this identity allowed to perform the action at this scope? Owner passes for almost everything.
- **Azure Policy**: does the resulting resource meet the assigned rules? This check ignores who is asking.
If a policy with the **Deny** effect matches, the request fails with HTTP 403 (Forbidden) and the error names the policy assignment that blocked it. Built-in definitions such as **Allowed storage account SKUs** work this way.
## RBAC plus Policy
Learn describes the two as complementary: RBAC manages user actions, Azure Policy manages resource state, and together they give full control. Holding a powerful role never exempts you from policy.
## Fixing it
Choose a permitted SKU, or ask the policy owner to change the assignment, add an exemption or exclude the scope.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Storage Account Contributor only:** Owner has full rights to create and manage all resources in its scope, including storage accounts, so the role is not the cause.
- ✗ **B. Lock approval:** locks block deletes or changes for everyone and have no approval workflow; the error message points to a policy, not a lock.
- ✗ **C. Budget exceeded:** Cost Management budgets send alerts (and can trigger action groups), but they never block resource creation, whatever the SKU.
- ✓ **D. Deny policy (correct):** a Deny effect rejects noncompliant create requests for everyone, including Owners, because Azure Policy evaluates the resource, not the caller's permissions.

## Key idea
A "disallowed by policy" error comes from an Azure Policy Deny assignment, which applies to every caller, even an Owner.
Q006549:
## Lock scopes and inheritance
Resource locks can be applied to a **subscription**, a **resource group** or a **single resource**. They cannot be added to management groups.
A lock on a parent scope is inherited by everything inside it, even resources created later, and the most restrictive lock in the chain wins.
## Who manages locks
Creating or deleting a lock needs the `Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*` permissions. The built-in **Owner** and **User Access Administrator** roles include them; a custom role can grant them too. A lock stays until someone with those permissions removes it.
## Two lock levels
- **Delete** (`CanNotDelete` on the command line): authorized users can still read and **modify** the resource, but nobody can delete it.
- **ReadOnly**: authorized users can read the resource but cannot update or delete it, much like restricting everyone to the Reader role.
Locks apply to every user and role and do not expire. They cover control plane operations (changes through Azure Resource Manager), not the data inside the resource.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Owner and User Access Administrator (correct):** these built-in roles hold the lock management permissions, so they can add and remove locks.
- ✗ **B. Delete lock blocks changes:** a Delete lock only prevents deletion; authorized users can still modify the VM, including resizing it. Blocking changes needs a ReadOnly lock.
- ✗ **C. Management group lock:** locks can be applied to subscriptions, resource groups and resources, but not to management groups.
- ✗ **D. Automatic expiry:** locks have no expiry date. A lock stays in place until a user with permission removes it.
- ✓ **E. Inherited by new resources (correct):** locks on a parent apply to all child resources, including ones created after the lock was set.

## Key idea
Locks are inherited from a subscription or resource group down to every resource, last until removed, and can be managed by Owners and User Access Administrators.
Q006550:
## Locks and resource group deletion
Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it. Azure Resource Manager checks locks on the group **and on every resource inside it** before doing anything.
Learn is explicit: if one resource has a Delete lock and you try to delete its resource group, the whole delete operation is blocked, even if the group and the other resources are unlocked. **A partial deletion isn't possible.**
## What to do
- Remove the lock from the VM (it needs `Microsoft.Authorization/locks` permissions, such as Owner or User Access Administrator), then delete the group, or
- Move the VM to another resource group first if it must survive, then delete the group.
## Related behavior
A Delete lock on a resource or resource group also stops role assignments on it from being deleted, and a Delete lock on a group stops Resource Manager from cleaning up old deployment history.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lock ignored:** a resource-level lock is exactly what stops the parent group from being deleted. It is not bypassed by deleting the parent.
- ✓ **B. Whole operation blocked (correct):** Resource Manager refuses the group deletion if any resource inside carries a Delete lock, and it never performs a partial delete.
- ✗ **C. Partial delete:** Learn states that partial deletion isn't possible; nothing is deleted when one resource is locked.
- ✗ **D. Automatic move:** Azure never moves resources on its own to work around a lock; moving the VM would be a manual step by the admin.

## Key idea
One Delete lock on any resource blocks deletion of its whole resource group; Azure never deletes part of the group.
Q006551:
## Control plane and data plane
Azure separates two kinds of operations:
- **Control plane**: managing the resource itself, sent to Azure Resource Manager at `https://management.azure.com` (create the server, change its settings, delete it).
- **Data plane**: using the service, sent to the service instance itself (run SQL statements against a database, upload a blob to `https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net`).
## What locks protect
Resource locks apply **only to control plane operations**. They protect a resource from being changed or deleted, but they do not restrict how the resource performs its function. Learn's own example: a ReadOnly lock on a SQL Database logical server protects it from deletion or modification, while data in the databases can still be created, updated and deleted.
The same applies to storage: a lock on a storage account does not protect the blobs, files, queues or tables inside it from data plane deletes.
## A caveat
Some operations that look like reads are control plane POST requests, and a ReadOnly lock blocks them. Learn's examples: listing a storage account's access keys, or starting and restarting a VM in a locked resource group. Check what a lock will block before applying it.
## Protecting data
To protect data, use data-level features (permissions in the database, backups, soft delete, immutability) rather than locks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Control plane only (correct):** the lock stops changes to the server resource through Resource Manager, but SQL inserts and updates are data plane operations and are not affected.
- ✗ **B. Firewall rules only:** a lock on the server covers the server and its child resources at the control plane; it is not limited to firewall rules.
- ✗ **C. Daily evaluation:** locks are not evaluated on a schedule. They take effect as soon as they are created; that delay describes Azure Policy compliance scans.
- ✗ **D. Owner bypass:** locks apply to every user and role, Owners included. The writes succeed because they are data operations, not because of a role.

## Key idea
Resource locks guard the resource (control plane), not the data inside it (data plane).
Q006552:
## When Azure Policy evaluates
Azure Policy does not check resources continuously in real time. Evaluation is triggered by specific events:
- a resource is **created or updated** in a scope that has an assignment
- a policy or initiative is **newly assigned** to a scope
- an assignment or its definition is **updated**
- a **policy exemption** is created, updated or deleted (the assignment is reevaluated for the exempted scope)
- the **standard compliance evaluation cycle**, which reevaluates all assignments once every 24 hours
- an **on-demand scan** started with Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, REST or other tooling
Large scopes can take time to finish, so compliance results appear after evaluation completes, not instantly.
## What does not trigger evaluation
Viewing a resource, collecting monitoring metrics or billing events do not create or update the resource through Azure Resource Manager, so they do not start a policy evaluation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Monitoring metrics:** CPU readings are telemetry collected by Azure Monitor; they do not change the VM's configuration in Resource Manager, so they are not an evaluation trigger.
- ✗ **B. Viewing a resource:** reads in the portal do not change the resource and are not an evaluation trigger.
- ✗ **C. Invoice generation:** billing events in Cost Management have no link to Azure Policy evaluation.
- ✓ **D. 24-hour cycle (correct):** every assignment is automatically reevaluated once every 24 hours, which keeps compliance data current.
- ✓ **E. New assignment (correct):** assigning a policy or initiative to a scope starts an evaluation of all resources in that scope, including existing ones.

## Key idea
Azure Policy evaluates on resource changes, new or changed assignments, a 24-hour cycle and on-demand scans.

## Tools for interacting with Azure
Azure offers several ways to manage the same resources:
- **Azure portal**: a web-based, unified console with a **graphical user interface**. You can build, manage and monitor everything from simple web apps to complex deployments, create **custom dashboards**, and configure accessibility options. It is the alternative to command-line tools.

## How Cloud Shell works
**Azure Cloud Shell** is an interactive, authenticated, browser-accessible terminal with **Bash** or **PowerShell**. Microsoft manages it, and it comes with the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell and other common tools preinstalled.
Each session runs on a **temporary host** provided per session and per user. When the session ends (including after a period without activity), that host goes away.
## Persisting files
To keep files between sessions, Cloud Shell uses an **Azure Files share** in a storage account you choose or create on first use:
- your `$HOME` directory (scripts, SSH keys, profile settings) is saved in a disk image stored in that share and synced automatically
- the share is also mounted as `clouddrive` inside `$HOME`
Use of the Cloud Shell host is free; the storage account is billed at normal storage rates. If you start Cloud Shell without a storage account, files do not survive the session.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Browser local storage:** Cloud Shell files live in Azure, not in the browser; that is why the same files appear from any device.
- ✗ **B. Host kept running:** the host is temporary and created per session; it is not kept running between sessions.
- ✓ **C. Azure Files share (correct):** Cloud Shell stores the $HOME disk image in a mounted Azure Files share, so scripts and keys are available again in every new session.
- ✗ **D. Arc-enabled server:** Azure Arc manages machines outside Azure and has no role in storing Cloud Shell files.

## Key idea
Cloud Shell sessions run on temporary hosts; files persist only through the Azure Files share mounted for $HOME.

## Cloud Shell identity
Azure Cloud Shell is **authenticated with your Azure credentials**. When you open it, it already knows who you are and what permissions you have; there is no separate service account with extra rights.
Every Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell command in Cloud Shell is sent to Azure Resource Manager as **you**, so Azure RBAC applies exactly as it does in the portal or on a local workstation.

**Reader** allows viewing resources but not changing them. Its only permission is `*/read`. Stopping a VM needs an action permission such as `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/deallocate/action` or `.../powerOff/action` (a POST request to Resource Manager), which Reader does not include, so the request is refused with an authorization error.

Bash (with the Azure CLI) and PowerShell (with Azure PowerShell) in Cloud Shell manage the same resources; switching shells changes the syntax, not the permissions.

- ✗ **A. Arc required:** Azure VMs are already Azure Resource Manager resources. Azure Arc is for machines outside Azure and is not needed here.
- ✓ **B. Her own identity (correct):** Cloud Shell runs commands as the signed-in user, and the Reader role does not allow stopping a VM, so Resource Manager denies the request.
- ✗ **C. PowerShell only:** both Cloud Shell experiences can manage VMs; the shell choice changes syntax, not permissions.
- ✗ **D. Read-only commands:** Cloud Shell runs any Azure CLI or PowerShell command the user is authorized for; a local install would hit the same RBAC check.

## Key idea
Cloud Shell acts with the signed-in user's own permissions; it never grants more than their Azure RBAC roles.

## Azure Arc
**Azure Arc** extends Azure management to resources outside Azure: on-premises, at the edge and in other clouds. It projects them into Azure Resource Manager so they can be managed as if they ran in Azure. Q006563:
## Projection into Azure Resource Manager
Azure Resource Manager is the management layer for everything in Azure. Azure Arc "projects" non-Azure resources into it: it creates an Azure **representation** of the server, cluster or data service, while the actual workload keeps running where it is.

- a resource in a resource group with its own Azure resource ID
- organization with management groups, resource groups and tags
- search and inventory with Azure Resource Graph
- access control with Azure RBAC and governance with Azure Policy
- monitoring, security and updates through Azure services (Azure Monitor, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Update Manager)

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Converted to Azure VM:** conversion into Azure VMs is migration. With Arc the server keeps running on its own hardware.
- ✓ **B. Azure representation (correct):** projection gives each server an Azure resource that can be organized, tagged, secured and governed with Azure tools, while the server itself stays on-premises.
- ✗ **C. Disk upload:** Arc does not copy server data into Azure; backing up data is the job of Azure Backup.

Azure Arc projection = an Azure Resource Manager representation of an outside resource, managed with Azure tools while it runs where it is.
Q006564:
## Maintenance as a cost factor
Microsoft lists **maintenance** as one of the factors that affect Azure cost. When you create a VM, Azure also creates supporting resources: an OS disk (and maybe data disks), a network interface, and often a public IP address.
These are separate resources with their own meters. When you delete the VM, those extra resources may not be deleted at the same time, either on purpose (you want to keep the disk) or by accident.
## Why it matters
Anything that still exists can still be billed. A forgotten disk or IP address quietly adds cost every month until someone removes it.
## Example
A resource group `rg-test` once held `vm-test01`. After the VM was deleted, `vm-test01_OsDisk` and `vm-test01-ip` are still listed. Cost analysis grouped by resource shows exactly these two lines, and deleting them (or the whole resource group, if nothing else is needed) stops the charges.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Fixed retention period:** Azure does not hold and later auto-delete a deleted VM's leftovers. They stay until someone removes them, so waiting will not stop the charges.
- ✗ **B. Resource group charge:** a resource group is a free logical container. The charges come from the resources inside it, here the disk and the IP address.
- ✓ **C. Leftover resources (correct):** a VM's disks, network interface and public IP address are separate resources. Deleting the VM does not always delete them, and each one that remains keeps its own charges, which is why cleaning up regularly is part of controlling cost.
- ✗ **D. Final compute charges:** compute for a deleted VM stops when the VM is gone; Cost Management reports meters per resource and does not relabel compute as disk or IP usage.

## Key idea
Deleting a VM may leave disks and IP addresses behind; regular cleanup of unused resources is part of cost control.
Q006565:
## Azure Marketplace
**Azure Marketplace** lets you buy Azure-based solutions from third-party vendors: a preconfigured web server, a VM with specialised software installed, a managed backup service and so on. Marketplace solutions are certified against Azure policies and standards.
## How it affects cost
When you deploy from Marketplace you can pay for two things:
- the **Azure resources** the solution uses (VM size, disks, networking), billed like any other resource;
- the **vendor's software or expertise**, with a billing structure the vendor sets (for example a per-hour software fee or a bring-your-own-license option).
## Example
Two VMs of the same size in the same region: one from a plain Linux image, one from a vendor's firewall image. Compute is the same, but the second line item adds the vendor's software charge, so the total is higher.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Automatic support plan:** a Marketplace purchase bills the Azure resources plus the vendor's own terms. It does not attach a Microsoft support plan to the subscription.
- ✗ **B. Premium capacity tier:** there is no special Marketplace compute tier. The VM size and region set the compute rate exactly as for any other VM.
- ✗ **C. Mandatory reservation:** Marketplace VMs can run pay-as-you-go. Reservations are an optional discount you choose, not a requirement of Marketplace images.
- ✓ **D. Vendor charges (correct):** buying through Azure Marketplace can add the third-party vendor's charges on top of the Azure infrastructure, and those billing terms come from the vendor, so the same VM size costs more with the vendor's product installed.

## Key idea
Azure Marketplace items can carry third-party vendor charges in addition to the Azure resources they run on.
Q006566:
## Subscription type as a cost factor
Microsoft lists **subscription type** among the factors that affect cost: some Azure subscription types include **usage allowances**.
- An **Azure free account** gives access to a set of products free for a limited period, a credit to spend shortly after sign-up, and a list of services that are always free within limits (based on resource and region availability).
- A **pay-as-you-go** subscription has no such allowance: you are billed for what you use in each billing cycle.
## What does not change
Two people can deploy the same service in the same region with the same settings. The resource, region and usage are identical; the subscription's allowance is what makes one bill zero and the other not, until the allowance runs out.
## Example
A student deploys a small database in a free account and stays within the free allowance, so nothing is billed. The same database in a pay-as-you-go subscription appears on the monthly invoice.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Subscription type (correct):** free accounts include allowances (free products, credit and always-free services within limits), while pay-as-you-go bills all usage, so the same workload can cost nothing in one subscription and appear on the bill in the other.
- ✗ **B. Azure Marketplace:** Marketplace can add vendor charges, but both people run ordinary Azure services with no vendor billing involved, so Marketplace cannot explain why only one of them pays.
- ✗ **C. Geography:** region does change prices, but free accounts are not restricted to special no-charge regions. The difference here comes from the allowance, not the location.
- ✗ **D. Maintenance:** maintenance is about removing resources you no longer need. Free accounts do not silently delete idle resources to avoid charges.

## Key idea
Subscription type matters because some subscriptions, such as the free account, include usage allowances that offset cost.
Q006567:
## Two different kinds of "zone"
Azure uses the word *zone* in two unrelated ways.
- **Availability zone**: physically separate datacenters within one region, each with independent power, cooling and networking. It is a resiliency concept.
- **Billing zone**: a geographical grouping of Azure regions used only for **data transfer pricing**. It is a billing concept.
## How billing zones affect cost
Bandwidth is data moving in and out of Azure datacenters. Some inbound transfers are free, while outbound transfers are priced by billing zone. That is why moving data within Europe costs less than moving it from Europe to Asia or South America.
## Example
Copying backups from a West Europe resource to North Europe stays within one geography and costs less than sending the same data to a region in another continent.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Billing zone (correct):** Microsoft defines it as a geographical grouping of regions for data transfer pricing, and states that billing zones are different from availability zones.
- ✗ **B. Availability zone:** this describes an availability zone, a resiliency feature inside one region. It plays no part in how outbound data transfer is priced.
- ✗ **C. Region pair:** this describes paired regions, which relate to update sequencing and recovery planning, not to data transfer price groups.
- ✗ **D. Resource group:** a container that groups resources is a resource group. It organises resources and does not define bandwidth prices.

## Key idea
A billing zone groups regions for data transfer pricing; it is unrelated to availability zones.
Q006568:
## Direction matters for bandwidth cost
**Bandwidth** in Azure means data moving into and out of Azure datacenters.
- **Inbound** (ingress, into Azure): some inbound data transfers are free.
- **Outbound** (egress, leaving Azure datacenters): priced based on **billing zones**, geographical groupings of regions.
The storage account still has its own charges (capacity, access tier, redundancy, operations), but the bandwidth part depends mainly on how much data leaves Azure and where it goes.
## Applying it
A workload that pushes a lot of data **in** and rarely pulls it **out**, such as an archive, has a low bandwidth cost. A workload that serves large downloads to users around the world has a higher one.
## Example
Uploading monthly archives to Blob Storage: little or no transfer charge. Restoring several archives to an on-premises site in another continent: outbound transfer charged by billing zone.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Same rate both ways:** inbound and outbound are not treated the same. Outbound is what is priced by billing zone, so upload volume is not the main bandwidth driver.
- ✗ **B. Availability zone pricing:** transfer prices are based on billing zones, which group regions. Availability zones are a resiliency feature and do not remove bandwidth charges.
- ✗ **C. Included in storage price:** data transfer is its own cost factor. Downloads out of Azure can appear as bandwidth charges in addition to storage charges.
- ✓ **D. Ingress versus egress (correct):** Microsoft states that some inbound transfers are free and outbound transfers are priced by zone. With heavy uploads and rare downloads, bandwidth is a small part of this workload's cost.

## Key idea
Data going into Azure is often free; data leaving Azure is what is priced by billing zone.

Q006570:
## One place for spending alerts
Cost Management's **cost alerts** view gathers the alerts that are about **money**. Microsoft lists three types:

- ✗ **B. Activity log alerts:** these Azure Monitor alerts react to operations like deleting a resource. They are about changes, not about spending.
- ✓ **C. Credit alerts (correct):** generated automatically as an EA's Azure Prepayment is used up; they appear in cost alerts and are emailed to account owners.
- ✗ **D. Service Health alerts:** these come from Azure Service Health through Azure Monitor and report platform incidents, not spending.

Q006571:
## Actual versus forecasted budget alerts
A **budget** in Cost Management sets a spending amount for a scope (such as a subscription or resource group) and a reset period (monthly, quarterly or annual). Each alert condition has a type:
- **Actual**: fires when the money already spent reaches the threshold, for example 80% of the budget.
- **Forecasted**: fires when Cost Management's cost **projection** for the period is expected to exceed the threshold. This gives advance notice while there is still time to act.
Either way the budget only notifies (and can call an action group); it does not stop resources by itself.
## Example
A monthly budget for `rg-project` with a forecasted alert at 100%: on day 10, spending is only 40% of the budget, but the trend projects 115% by month end, so the manager is warned on day 10 instead of on day 27.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Forecasted alert (correct):** forecasted budget alerts use cost predictions and fire when the projected spend for the period passes the threshold, so the manager hears about the trend before the money is actually spent.
- ✗ **B. Advisor recommendation:** Advisor suggests savings such as resizing idle VMs. It does not compare month-to-date spending with a budget or send budget warnings.
- ✗ **C. Credit alert:** credit alerts track an Enterprise Agreement's Azure Prepayment balance. They are not tied to a project budget or its trend.
- ✗ **D. Actual alert at 100%:** an actual-cost alert fires only when real spending reaches the threshold. At 100% the budget has already been spent, which is too late for this requirement.

## Key idea
Use a forecasted budget alert to be warned before spending actually exceeds a budget.

Q006573:

Q006574:
## Designing a tag schema
A **tag** is a name and a value, such as `Impact=Mission-critical` or `CostCenter=4100`. You can assign one or more tags to each resource, and you can add, change or delete them at any time through the portal, PowerShell, the Azure CLI, ARM templates or the REST API.
Tags are metadata only: they describe resources and drive reports and automation, but they do not change how a resource runs or what it costs.
## Not every tag belongs on every resource
Microsoft's guidance is that you do **not** need to enforce that a specific tag is present on all resources. An `Impact` tag might be placed only on mission-critical resources; every resource without it is then treated as not mission-critical.
If a tag must be present everywhere (for example `Owner` or `CostCenter`), you can make it mandatory with **Azure Policy**, but that is a choice you make, not a built-in rule.
## Example
Only 120 production resources get `Impact=Mission-critical`. A filter on that tag lists them for the on-call team, and the other 1,880 resources need no change.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Tags only at creation:** tags can be added, modified or removed on existing resources at any time, so no redeployment is needed.
- ✓ **B. Optional tags (correct):** each resource can carry its own set of tags, and Microsoft notes that a tag such as Impact can be applied only to mission-critical resources, with untagged resources treated as not mission-critical. This avoids tagging 2,000 resources for no benefit.
- ✗ **C. Same tag names everywhere:** Azure has no rule that all resources share one tag set. Requiring a tag is something you choose to enforce, for example with Azure Policy.
- ✗ **D. Higher service level:** tags are descriptive metadata. They do not change a resource's service level or price, so a tag on a test resource costs nothing extra.

## Key idea
Tags are optional per resource: apply a tag such as Impact only where it is meaningful, and use Azure Policy only for tags that must be everywhere.
Q006575:
## Tags for automation
Tags add metadata to resources, and Microsoft lists **workload optimisation and automation** among their uses: you can tag resources with their environment, workload or application name, then let automation tools find and act on them.
Because tags cut across resource groups and subscriptions, they work even when resources are mixed together and cannot be reorganised.

- Tag: `Environment=Dev` or `Environment=Test`.

## Why each option works or fails

- ✗ **B. Separate region:** moving VMs to another region is a large migration that can change cost and latency. It is far from the simplest way to label a set of VMs.
- ✗ **C. Budget per resource group:** budgets send alerts about spending; they do not run on a nightly schedule or pick out non-production VMs.
- ✓ **D. Environment tag (correct):** a tag can be read by scripts and automation in any resource group or subscription, so the job can pick exactly the Dev and Test VMs without moving anything.

Tags label resources across resource groups and subscriptions so that automation can target them, for example stopping all Environment=Dev VMs.
Q006576:
## What tags are for
A **tag** is metadata: a name and a value attached to a resource, resource group or subscription. Microsoft lists these uses:
- **Resource management**: find resources by workload, environment, team or owner.
- **Cost management and optimisation**: report on costs, allocate cost centres, track budgets.
- **Operations management**: group resources by how critical their availability is, which helps when you define service levels.
- **Security**: classify data by security level, such as public or confidential.
- **Governance and compliance**: identify resources that must meet requirements such as ISO 27001.
- **Workload optimisation and automation**: drive scripts and DevOps tasks.
## What tags do not do
Tags describe; they do not enforce. A tag does not block deletion (that is a resource lock), does not encrypt anything, and does not change the price of a resource. You also do not have to put every tag on every resource: an `Impact` tag might go only on mission-critical resources.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Operational criticality (correct):** tags can group resources by how critical their availability is, such as `Impact=Mission-critical`, which helps plan operations and service levels.
- ✗ **B. Encryption by tag:** tags do not encrypt data or choose keys. Encryption is a setting of the service, such as encryption at rest in Azure Storage.
- ✗ **C. Lower hourly rate:** tags are free metadata and do not change what a resource costs; prices come from the resource type, settings, region and usage.
- ✗ **D. Blocking deletion:** preventing deletion is the job of a resource lock. A tag value like Prod is only a label; any blocking comes from a lock or a policy rule, not from the tag itself.
- ✓ **E. Security classification (correct):** tags can mark the security level of the data a resource holds, for example `Classification=Confidential`.

## Key idea
Tags are descriptive metadata used for cost, operations, security classification, compliance and automation; they do not enforce, encrypt or change prices.
Q006577:
## Ways to buy compute
The **consumption** cost factor is about how much you use and also how you pay for it.
- **Pay-as-you-go**: no commitment; each hour of use is billed at the standard rate. Most flexible, no discount.
- **Reservations**: commit to specific resources (for example a VM size in a region) for one or three years. Best for stable workloads that run continuously.
- **Azure savings plan for compute**: commit to an **hourly spend amount** on eligible compute for one or three years. Suits steady spend that moves between VM types or services. Unused commitment in an hour does not roll over.
- **Azure Spot Virtual Machines**: use **unused Azure capacity** at lower prices. Azure can **evict** them when it needs the capacity back, and there is no SLA, so they suit work that tolerates interruption, such as batch processing and dev/test.
## Matching the workload
Commitments pay off when usage is steady around the clock. A job that runs only at night and can restart after an interruption gets the most from Spot.
## Example
A render job checkpoints every frame. Overnight two Spot VMs are evicted; the scheduler starts new ones and the job resumes from the last saved frame, at a fraction of the on-demand cost.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reservations:** a reservation is a commitment for continuous use of specific capacity. VMs that sit idle all day would waste most of the reserved hours.
- ✓ **B. Spot Virtual Machines (correct):** Microsoft recommends Spot for workloads that can handle interruptions, such as batch jobs. The render jobs checkpoint and restart, so eviction only delays them, and the studio pays the lower Spot price instead of the standard rate.
- ✗ **C. Pay-as-you-go:** it fits the part-time schedule but charges the full on-demand rate, so it costs more than Spot for interruptible work.
- ✗ **D. Savings plan:** the hourly commitment applies to every hour of the term, and unused commitment does not roll over, so a night-only workload leaves much of it unused.

## Key idea
Interruptible, restartable work such as batch rendering fits Azure Spot Virtual Machines; commitments fit steady around-the-clock usage.
Q006578:
## What the pricing calculator is
The **Azure pricing calculator** is a web tool for estimating the cost of Azure resources **before** you deploy them. You can price a single resource, build a full solution, or start from an example scenario. It covers compute, storage and associated network costs, and options such as storage type, access tier and redundancy.
## What it is not
